items.title: How Ansible works
items.context: Ansible is agentless: a control node connects to managed hosts over SSH (WinRM for Windows) and pushes small modules that run and report back. Hosts only need SSH and Python.

questions.prompt: What must you install on managed Linux hosts for Ansible?
choices: Nothing special — SSH access and Python
questions.explanation: That's the agentless model, unlike Puppet or Chef agents.

items.title: Inventory
items.context: The inventory lists hosts and groups (INI or YAML, static or dynamic from a cloud API). Playbooks target groups: hosts: webservers. Group and host variables live in group_vars/ and host_vars/.

questions.prompt: Where do you declare that web1 and web2 belong to the webservers group?
questions.explanation: Dynamic inventories build this from cloud tags.

items.title: Idempotency
items.context: An idempotent task produces the same result however many times it runs, and reports 'changed' only when it actually changed something. Built-in modules (apt, copy, template, service) are idempotent; shell and command aren't unless you add creates: or changed_when:.

questions.prompt: Installing nginx, which task is idempotent?
choices: shell: apt-get install -y nginx && echo done
questions.explanation: The apt module checks first and only installs if nginx is missing.

items.title: Handlers
items.context: Handlers are tasks that run only when notified by a task that changed something, and they run once at the end of the play, even if notified many times. The classic case is restarting a service after its config file changes.

questions.prompt: Three tasks notify 'restart nginx' and all three change something. The handler runs:
choices: Once, at the end of the play
questions.explanation: Use meta: flush_handlers to run pending handlers earlier.

items.title: Roles
items.context: Roles package reusable automation in a standard layout: tasks/, handlers/, templates/, files/, defaults/ and vars/. They're shared through Ansible Galaxy or collections and applied with roles: or include_role.

questions.prompt: In a role, the lowest-precedence, easy-to-override variables go in:
questions.explanation: vars/ has much higher precedence, so put overridable settings in defaults/.

items.title: Variable precedence
items.context: Ansible has many variable sources with a fixed precedence. Role defaults are the lowest; extra vars passed with -e on the command line are the highest and override everything else.

questions.prompt: Which always wins?
choices: Extra vars (-e on the command line)
questions.explanation: Useful for one-off overrides in CI, e.g. -e version=1.4.2.

items.title: Templates
items.context: The template module renders Jinja2 files ({{ variable }}, {% for %} loops) with your variables and copies the result to the host — ideal for config files that differ per environment.

questions.prompt: Which templating language does the template module use?
questions.explanation: Files usually end in .j2.

items.title: Ansible Vault
items.context: ansible-vault encrypts files or single variables (AES-256) so secrets can live in the repository. Playbooks decrypt them at run time with a vault password, prompted or supplied from a file or script.

questions.prompt: You need a database password in the repository for a playbook. Use:
choices: A plain YAML file in group_vars
questions.explanation: Or fetch it at run time from a secrets manager lookup.

items.title: Dry runs
items.context: ansible-playbook --check runs without making changes and predicts what would change; --diff shows line-by-line differences for files and templates. Modules that don't support check mode are skipped.

questions.prompt: Which flags preview a playbook's changes, including file differences?
questions.explanation: --syntax-check only parses the playbook.

items.title: Ansible vs Terraform
items.context: Terraform excels at provisioning cloud resources declaratively and tracks them in state. Ansible excels at configuring what runs inside machines (packages, files, services) and at orchestration, with no state file. Many teams use Terraform to create servers and Ansible to configure them.

questions.prompt: A sensible split for 'create 3 VMs on AWS and install a hardened nginx on them' is:
choices: Terraform creates the VMs; Ansible configures them
questions.explanation: Use each tool where its model fits; Terraform itself discourages provisioners.

items.title: Ad-hoc commands
items.context: ansible <pattern> -m <module> -a '<args>' runs a single module without a playbook: ansible all -m ping checks connectivity; ansible web -m service -a 'name=nginx state=restarted' restarts nginx.

questions.prompt: Quickest way to check Ansible can reach every host:
questions.explanation: The ping module checks SSH and Python, not ICMP.

items.title: Privilege escalation
items.context: become: true runs tasks with sudo (become_user defaults to root); set it per play or per task.

questions.prompt: A task installing packages needs root. Add:
questions.explanation: Keep it to the tasks that need it.

items.title: Facts
items.context: With gather_facts on (the default), Ansible collects host details at the start of a play: OS family, distribution, IP addresses, memory. Use them as ansible_facts['os_family'] in conditions and templates.

questions.prompt: To install with apt only on Debian-family hosts, test:
questions.explanation: Facts come from the setup module.

items.title: Loops
items.context: loop: repeats a task over a list, with the current value in {{ item }} — e.g. install several packages or create several users. Many modules also accept lists directly (apt: name=[git, curl]), which is faster.

questions.prompt: Inside a looped task, the current element is:
questions.explanation: loop_control: loop_var renames it when nesting.

items.title: Conditionals
items.context: when: runs a task only if an expression is true — e.g. when: ansible_facts['os_family'] == 'RedHat' or when: result.rc != 0. It's raw Jinja2, so no {{ }} braces.

questions.prompt: Which skips a task on non-production hosts?
questions.explanation: Conditions can use facts, variables and registered results.

items.title: register & debug
items.context: register: saves a task's result (stdout, rc, changed…) into a variable for later tasks; the debug module prints variables while developing: debug: var=result.

questions.prompt: How do you use a command's output in a later task?
choices: Write it to a temp file by hand
questions.explanation: Combine with when: to branch on results.

items.title: Tags
items.context: Tag tasks or roles (tags: [nginx]) and run a subset with --tags nginx or skip some with --skip-tags.

questions.prompt: Run only the tasks tagged 'certs':
questions.explanation: Useful for long playbooks.

items.title: Rolling updates with serial
items.context: serial: 2 (or a percentage such as 25%) makes a play run on hosts in batches, so a deploy rolls through the fleet instead of hitting every server at once; max_fail_percentage stops a bad rollout early.

questions.prompt: Deploy to 2 web servers at a time to keep the site up:
questions.explanation: forks controls parallel connections, not rollout batches.

items.title: delegate_to
items.context: delegate_to: runs a task on a different host than the one being processed — e.g. removing each web server from the load balancer pool (on the LB host) before updating it, then adding it back.

questions.prompt: Take each app server out of the load balancer during its update:
choices: Use a handler on the LB
Tasks with delegate_to: <lb host> before and after the update, with serial: 1
questions.explanation: Classic zero-downtime pattern.

items.title: Collections & Galaxy
items.context: Modules beyond the core are distributed as collections (amazon.aws, community.general, kubernetes.core) installed with ansible-galaxy collection install, ideally pinned in requirements.yml.

questions.prompt: How do you install the amazon.aws modules?
questions.explanation: Pin versions in requirements.yml for repeatable runs.
